Empirical Research Plan: The Labor-Market Returns to Compulsory Schooling in Germany  

-------------------------------------------------------------

1. Identification Strategy  
Choice: Instrumental‐Variables (2SLS) design combined with a staggered Difference-in-Differences / event-study first stage.  
Justification  
• The reforms mandated an exogenous increase in minimum schooling that varies by state (Bundesland) and birth cohort.  
• The main causal parameter of interest is the effect of an additional year of schooling (a continuous treatment) on earnings and employment. Using the reform indicator as an instrument for actual years of education yields a clean Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) for compliers (those whose education changed because of the mandate).  
• A two-way-fixed-effects DID / event study validates the first-stage relevance and the parallel-trends assumption.  

2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment variable  
Tsi = 1 if individual i born in state s belongs to the first (and later) cohorts required to complete the extra year because of the law change implemented in state s; 0 otherwise.  

Control group  
• Within-state cohorts born just before the reform cutoff who faced the old requirement.  
• Cohorts in states that had not yet implemented the reform serve as additional controls (difference-in-differences in both time and space).  

Treatment timing  
Let bs be the first birth year fully exposed in state s (first school entry cohort after the law was enacted). Individuals with birth year ≥ bs are “treated.”  

Running variable and cutoff  
Not an RDD; running variable is year of birth, but treatment is discrete at the reform threshold and therefore fits a DID / IV framework, not RDD.  

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
A1. Policy Exogeneity: Timing of reforms is orthogonal to unobserved determinants of earnings/employment at the cohort-state level. Plausible—schooling‐law changes reflected national education harmonisation goals, not local labour-market shocks.  
A2. Parallel Trends (reduced form): In absence of the reform, labour-market outcomes of adjacent cohorts would have evolved similarly across states. Plausible if we include rich state and cohort fixed effects and test pre-trends.  
A3. First-Stage Relevance: The law actually increased mean years of schooling. Historically documented; will be confirmed empirically.  
A4. Exclusion Restriction: The reform affects outcomes only through additional schooling (no direct effects). Plausible but threatened by changes in school quality or tracking age; we will probe robustness (see Section 4).  
A5. Monotonicity: No one reduced schooling because of the increased minimum (no “defiers”). Reasonable—law raised the lower bound.  

4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  
T1. Selective Migration of families around reform dates.  
   • Restrict to individuals who attended school in their birth state (GSOEP reports this).  
   • Show that parental socioeconomic characteristics do not jump at the cutoff.  
T2. Concurrent state-level policies (vocational training reforms, regional shocks).  
   • Control for state-specific linear or quadratic cohort trends.  
   • Add time-varying state controls (unemployment rate, GDP per capita).  
   • Run event-study plots to check for other discontinuities.  
T3. TWFE negative-weight bias with staggered adoption.  
   • Implement Sun & Abraham (2021) or Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021) estimators for reduced-form and first stage; then combine into Wald LATE.  
   • Report Goodman-Bacon decomposition to show weight structure.  

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# ----------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)        # fast FELM & IV
library(did)           # Callaway & Sant'Anna
library(bacondecomp)   # Goodman-Bacon weights
# ----------------------------------------------
# 1. Load and clean data
gsoep <- read_csv("GSOEP_compulsory_schooling.csv") %>%
  mutate(
    yob      = birth_year,
    state    = factor(state_of_schooling),
    cohort   = yob,
    # construct treatment: exposed if born in or after first affected cohort
    treat    = as.integer(yob >= reform_first_affected_cohort &
                          yob <= reform_first_affected_cohort + 10), # +/- window
    yearsedu = years_of_schooling,
    ln_earn  = log(real_annual_earnings),
    employed = as.integer(employment_status == "employed")
  ) %>%
  # drop missing key variables
  drop_na(yearsedu, ln_earn, employed, treat)

# ----------------------------------------------
# 2. Main 2SLS specification
#   ln_earn_{i} = β * yearsedu_{i} + γ'X + α_state + δ_cohort + ε
#   yearsedu_{i} instrumented by treat
iv_main <- feols(
  ln_earn ~ 1 | state + cohort | (yearsedu ~ treat) | state,
  data = gsoep,
  cluster = ~state
)
summary(iv_main)

# Employment outcome
iv_emp <- feols(
  employed ~ 1 | state + cohort | (yearsedu ~ treat) | state,
  data = gsoep,
  cluster = ~state
)

# ----------------------------------------------
# 3. Event-study / dynamic DID (robustness)
did_cs <- att_gt(
  yname   = "ln_earn",
  tname   = "cohort",
  idname  = "id_person",
  gname   = "reform_first_affected_cohort",  # timing of treatment
  xformla = ~ sex + foreign + parental_edu,
  data    = gsoep,
  est_method = "dr"
)
es_plot <- ggdid(event_study(did_cs))

# ----------------------------------------------
# 4. Goodman-Bacon decomposition check
bacon_out <- bacon(ln_earn ~ treat, data = gsoep,
                   id_var = "state", time_var = "cohort")
plot(bacon_out)

# ----------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: drop movers
gsoep_nomovers <- gsoep %>% filter(moved_state == 0)
iv_nomovers <- feols(
  ln_earn ~ 1 | state + cohort | (yearsedu ~ treat) | state,
  data = gsoep_nomovers,
  cluster = ~state
)
summary(iv_nomovers)
```

6. Expected Results  
Direction: Positive. Human-capital theory predicts that an extra mandatory year raises productivity, hence wages and the likelihood of employment.  
Magnitude: Prior work in Europe finds ≈ 8–10% increase in earnings per additional year. Given Germany’s extensive vocational system the return may be slightly lower, say 5–8% in log wages (β ≈ 0.05–0.08). Employment probability expected to rise by 1–3 percentage points.  

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV with policy shocks)  
C1. Relevance of instrument: 1 (strongly satisfied)  
C2. Exogeneity / parallel trends: 0.8 (mostly satisfied; will test)  
C3. Exclusion restriction: 0.6 (some concern about simultaneous quality changes)  
C4. No selective migration / manipulation: 0.7 (plausible but testable)  
C5. Monotonicity & SUTVA: 1 (clearly satisfied)  

Overall score ≈ 4.1 / 5 → credible but warrants robustness checks.
